title: Lombardelli explains why weak hiring has yet to dislodge her case for another rise
summary: Clare Lombardelli sees a particular risk in treating rising UK unemployment as a reliable measure of forthcoming wage disinflation. Employers have cut vacancies much more than existing jobs. The workers struggling hardest to find a position are disproportionately young and concentrated in sectors with fewer openings. If they cannot compete quickly for the jobs where recruitment remains difficult, their unemployment may do less to restrain pay elsewhere. The Deputy Governor judged the risks to inflation tilted upward and saw a likely case for another near-term rate increase absent evidence that inflationary pressure was weakening. That was her conditional judgment on 10 November. The collective action she cited was the preceding week’s 8–1 MPC vote to raise Bank Rate by 25 basis points to 4%.

Start with the scale of the slowdown. Unemployment rose from below 4% in 2022 to above 5% late in 2025, then fell to 4.7% in the three months to August. During six consecutive quarters from mid-2024 it rose by about one percentage point, considerably less abrupt than past recessionary increases. In the November central projection it remained around 5%. Output had also been stronger and unemployment lower than in the middle of the three April scenarios drawn up soon after the conflict began. April had no central projection. Treating the difference between those two paths as an ordinary revision between successive central forecasts would overstate the comparability.

The composition of adjustment is clearer than the unemployment total. The Labour Force Survey redundancy rate was close to its pre-pandemic level. Notifications of proposed redundancies and other measures provided corroboration, while vacancies were below their pre-pandemic level and the REC staffing-demand measure remained below 50. In Chart 5 most of the recent rise in unemployment is attributed to weaker job finding. Its estimate uses changes in unemployment by duration to infer hiring and separation rates; the chart’s reconstructed unemployment rate can differ from the published headline. Lombardelli also flags continuing caution about the Labour Force Survey. The contrast between hiring and redundancies rests on several sources with different measurement issues, a stronger basis than a single monthly estimate.

Retaining skilled employees has an option value for firms that remember post-pandemic shortages. With demand uncertain and energy costs higher, firms could trim recruitment and temporarily absorb costs in margins. Chart 9’s survey balances show opposite directions for prices and margins, and weaker employment and sales volumes. A net balance gives the direction across respondents rather than the percentage change in aggregate profits or jobs. Bank Agents heard plans to restore margins through higher prices, procurement savings and automation. The mechanism changes if elevated costs outlast the margin buffer: businesses could reduce existing employment and household demand more sharply. Firms’ willingness to wait helps explain why a relatively stable headcount can accompany a difficult entry market.

The cyclical weakness overlays a much longer decline in mobility. More than 3% of employed people moved directly between jobs each quarter around thirty years ago, against a little over 2% recently, close to financial-crisis lows despite less aggregate weakness. Chart 10 compares the observed rate with a cycle adjustment estimated over 1995–2019 and smooths the data over four quarters. The share of switches crossing industry boundaries was above one half in the early 2000s, fell by roughly ten percentage points during the financial crisis and did not recover. Moves across broad occupational skill groups also became less common, with classification changes in 2011 and 2021 requiring care. Even so, nearly three million people switched jobs during 2025. Summed quarterly flows can include the same individual twice. A declining switching rate and substantial gross worker movement can both be true.

Young people reveal where the aggregate loses information. People aged 16–24 represented about one eighth of the labour force but more than half the increase in unemployment since mid-2022, and around 40% of the stock of unemployment. Their jobless rate was more than three times the aggregate rate. Compared with just before the pandemic, vacancies fell about 14% economy-wide, 19% in accommodation and food services and 46% in retail. Those industries supply many first jobs. Chart 17 compares the shares of vacancies and jobseekers across industries, assigning first-time entrants to industries using the recent entry patterns of comparable people. Their intended industry is estimated. This evidence supports a mismatch explanation without proving that each affected jobseeker turned down a vacancy in another industry.

The speech considers explanations on both sides of the labour market. Disrupted education, poor health, the mentoring required by new workers, higher relative minimum wages and uncertainty all affect entry. Around 29% of employers affected by the National Living Wage told the Bank’s survey they would lower total employment in response. That is a stated intention for overall jobs, not a realised youth-employment elasticity. A weaker inflow into work can leave lasting damage if young people miss early opportunities to acquire skills. On the other hand, fewer moves need not always lower welfare: better recruitment could eliminate brief unsuccessful matches. Lombardelli weighs that explanation against evidence of worse matching, lower job satisfaction and fewer chances of progression.

For inflation, the open question is how much of apparent slack is readily available to employers. Pay increases had moderated, but underlying pay was judged close to the upper end of the range consistent with the target and forward indicators suggested continuing pressure. A persistent deterioration in matching could temporarily raise equilibrium unemployment and shrink the disinflationary gap. Lombardelli explicitly said that the moderate increase in unemployment to date had not convinced her that the equilibrium rate had changed materially. She wants to see what happens to pay if unemployment increases further. This is a testable conditional hypothesis about matching and wage setting, rather than a new numerical estimate of equilibrium unemployment.

Mobility also affects the economy’s productive capacity. Better matches can raise workers’ pay together with output per worker; not every wage gain from switching is inflationary. Bank staff estimated that a group of AI-related industries contributed about 0.5 percentage points to UK gross value added growth from the start of 2026. Relative to their customary contribution, the excess was around 0.3 percentage points, just under one fifth of total growth. Chart 19 covers January through August. The proxy includes some unrelated technology activity and omits some AI-related construction and research. It measures sectoral output, not the causal gain from AI productivity. Firms surveyed expected future productivity gains through both higher output and lower employment. If the loss of entry-level tasks precedes new opportunities, a transition can produce more unemployment without immediate broad disinflation.

Her near-term policy judgment turns on four channels in Table A. Direct fuel and utility effects typically last up to a year and can be looked through. Indirect supply-chain effects can build over two years; whether they warrant a response depends on their persistence. Inflation expectations, wage bargaining and subsequent price setting can transmit second-round effects over as much as three years. The loss of household purchasing power works the other way through weaker demand over a similar horizon. Relative to July, energy prices had risen further and remained elevated for longer, while spending and activity had held up better than she expected. Indirect effects were still limited, second-round effects had not been demonstrated, and the disinflationary demand offset had been smaller than feared. The changing balance, together with indications that underlying disinflation had stalled, explains the case for the November increase and her willingness to consider another. A later collapse in spending or broader evidence that wage and pricing pressures were subsiding would change that balance. She advocates gradual decisions under uncertainty, without committing to a meeting date or a terminal rate.

questions.question: Is a given rise in unemployment now buying less wage disinflation because of mismatch?
questions.detail: Track the subsequent growth of settlements, regular private pay and firms’ own wage expectations alongside job-finding and separation rates. Compare industries where vacancies remained elevated with retail and other entry-intensive sectors, allowing for their different energy exposure and initial wage trends. Aggregate unemployment rising while sector-specific hiring difficulties and pay persist would strengthen the mismatch explanation. If pay weakens across sectors as vacancies fall, ordinary cyclical demand weakness could account for much of the evidence.

questions.question: When does absorbing energy costs in margins give way to layoffs or price increases?
questions.detail: Use repeated business-survey answers and Agents’ evidence to distinguish higher selling prices, efficiency savings and lower employment. Trace the sequence from restrained hiring to possible redundancies and compare energy-intensive and less exposed employers. A decline in sales with unchanged pricing and greater actual layoffs would strengthen the speech’s downside scenario. A larger reported energy bill alongside recovering margins and rising selling prices would instead point towards the indirect inflation channel.

questions.question: How much of the decline in youth entry reflects the absence of starter jobs rather than a lasting fall in capacity?
questions.detail: Match vacancy and first-hire data by sector, locality and age, maintaining consistent definitions across the pandemic and occupational reclassifications. Observe whether hiring resumes as sectoral demand recovers, and whether young entrants then move into ordinary progression and wage paths. Persistently lower employment and pay after comparable vacancies return would be more consistent with skill loss or matching frictions. Track the uncertainty around assigning industries to people who have never worked.

questions.question: Would more resilient activity justify a further rise if the composition of that activity changes?
questions.detail: Reassess her four channels jointly using the energy path, realised indirect price changes, settlements and household spending that were observable before the next decision. If a disproportionate share of additional output comes from higher productive capacity rather than demand for constrained resources, headline activity alone overstates the policy implication. Conversely, resilient demand, slower wage disinflation and firmer pricing expectations would fit her conditional case even without another jump in headline energy prices.

limitation: The forward policy judgment belongs to Clare Lombardelli. The speech’s flow decomposition, counterfactual scenarios and AI sector proxy are estimated quantities. The charts and tables do not identify a causal wage or market-price effect.
